prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, but must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. A Plaintiff Need Not Plead a Prima Facie Case to Survive a Rule 12(b)(6) Motion; She Must Allege Facts That Plausibly Support an Inference of Discrimination.

The district court dismissed the complaint because it did not establish each element of the *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie case. That was error. The *McDonnell Douglas* framework is "an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). This Court has repeatedly applied that rule. *See Coleman v. Md. Ct. of Appeals*, 626 F.3d 187, 190 (4th Cir. 2010), *aff'd*, 566 U.S. 30 (2012); *Goode v. Cent. Va. Legal Aid Soc'y, Inc.*, 807 F.3d 619, 626 (4th Cir. 2015); *McCleary-Evans v. Md. Dep't of Transp., State Highway Admin.*, 780 F.3d 582, 584 (4th Cir. 2015); *Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 648 (4th Cir. 2017); *Bing v. Brivo Sys., LLC*, 959 F.3d 605, 616–17 (4th Cir. 2020).

*Swierkiewicz* explained why. The prima facie case is a flexible evidentiary device that varies with the facts, and it does not set the outer limit of what a plaintiff must plead. 534 U.S. at 511–12. Requiring a plaintiff to plead each element before discovery would also demand proof of facts, such as the employer's treatment of comparators or its internal reasons for acting, that are typically in the defendant's hands. *Id.* at 512. *Twombly* and *Iqbal* did not displace this rule. Both decisions reaffirmed that Rule 8 demands "enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face," not a showing of evidentiary elements. *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007); *see Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678–79 (2009). This Court has confirmed that the two lines of authority operate together. *Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190; *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648.

The governing question is therefore not whether the complaint recites every element of a prima facie case. It is whether the complaint alleges facts that, taken as true, plausibly support the ultimate element of a discrimination claim: that the employer took adverse action *because of* a protected characteristic. *McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 585 (plaintiff must "allege facts to satisfy the elements of a cause of action created by [the] statute"); *Bing*, 959 F.3d at 617. At this stage, the Court accepts well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor. *Nemet Chevrolet, Ltd. v. Consumeraffairs.com, Inc.*, 591 F.3d 250, 255 (4th Cir. 2009). The Court does not credit bare legal conclusions or "naked assertion[s]" devoid of factual enhancement. *Francis v. Giacomelli*, 588 F.3d 186, 193 (4th Cir. 2009). Nor does it weigh competing explanations. A complaint is not implausible merely because the defendant can offer an innocent account. *See Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648–49; *Bing*, 959 F.3d at 617–18.

Measured against that standard, the complaint here suffices. This Court has dismissed discrimination complaints that rest on the plaintiff's subjective belief and offer no facts connecting the adverse action to a protected trait. *McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 585–86. The complaint here alleges concrete facts that tie the adverse action to Plaintiff's protected status. [*Insert record-specific allegations*: e.g., the decisionmaker's statements or conduct, the timing of the action, the treatment of similarly situated employees outside the protected class, and any departures from ordinary procedure. (J.A. __.)] Those allegations are not "conclusory" or based on speculation. They are specific facts that, taken together, "nudge[]" the claim "across the line from conceivable to plausible." *Twombly*, 550 U.S. at 570.

The district court's contrary conclusion rested on its finding that Plaintiff had not pleaded [*the element(s) the district court found lacking*]. That approach inverted the inquiry. Even if a particular prima facie element were not pleaded with precision, the question under *Swierkiewicz* and this Court's precedents is whether the facts alleged, viewed as a whole, permit a reasonable inference of discriminatory motive. *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648; *Bing*, 959 F.3d at 616–17. They do. Whether Plaintiff can ultimately carry her burden under *McDonnell Douglas* is a question for summary judgment or trial, after discovery.

The dismissal should be reversed.
